query: Prior studies of Al-containing Cr–Co–Fe–Ni alloys showed that composition and thermal history can substantially alter constituent phases and transformation behavior, but they did not establish a predictive explanation of phase stability across the relevant thermal regime or adequately connect it to composition-dependent thermodynamic instability. Given the competing thermodynamic and kinetic factors in multicomponent alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state and why? State a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations, boundary conditions, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7, phase stability is governed by a thermodynamic competition between high-temperature configurational entropy, which stabilizes the BCC phase, and the free-energy lowering induced by local chemical ordering upon cooling. In particular, negative mixing enthalpies between Al and the transition metals drive the formation of short-range ordered domains that mediate the transformation from the metastable high-temperature BCC state to lower-energy phase assemblages.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy in a high-temperature, entropy‐stabilized BCC state.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled thermal treatments varying cooling rates (rapid quench versus slow cooling with extended annealing) under otherwise identical conditions.
generation.conditions: The experiment will compare samples with identical composition starting from the same as-cast high-temperature BCC state. Testing will occur in a thermal regime where diffusion is active enough to enable local ordering (e.g., annealing just below the BCC stability limit) while avoiding mechanical deformation that could confound transformation kinetics.
generation.structural_mediator: The emergence of short-range chemical ordering, particularly involving Al-transition metal interactions, which locally lowers the free energy and provides nucleation sites for secondary phase formation.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, the alloy is stabilized in the BCC state by high configurational entropy. Upon cooling, the negative mixing enthalpies (especially involving Al with other species) favor the formation of locally ordered clusters. These chemically ordered regions lower the free energy relative to the disordered BCC phase, driving a transformation toward more thermodynamically favorable phase assemblages. The rate of cooling controls the kinetics of ordering; slow cooling permits more pronounced local ordering and phase transformation, while rapid quenching suppresses them.
generation.predicted_outcome: Slow-cooled samples will exhibit measurable local chemical ordering (detectable via techniques like TEM or atom probe tomography) and an increased content of secondary phases or precipitates relative to samples that are rapidly quenched. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) will reveal a transformation signature corresponding to the onset of ordering in the slow-cooled condition, which is absent or diminished in quenched samples.
generation.baseline: The as-cast high-temperature BCC state of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 will serve as the baseline microstructure and phase composition, against which changes induced by different cooling regimes are compared.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold within a temperature window where atomic diffusion is sufficiently active but not so rapid as to achieve full equilibrium, and for cooling rates that are not extreme (i.e., not so fast as to completely freeze-in the high-temperature state or so slow as to allow complete equilibration with possible segregation effects). It may not apply if extrinsic factors (such as significant mechanical deformation) dominate the transformation process.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative free energy differences and kinetics of short-range ordering remain uncertain until experimentally measured; local compositional fluctuations may also influence the extent and nature of chemical ordering.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy samples with identical composition and initial high-temperature BCC state. Divide the samples into two groups: one that is rapidly quenched and another that is slowly cooled with extended annealing near the predicted ordering temperature. Ensure that no mechanical deformation is applied. Characterize the resulting microstructure and phase composition using XRD, TEM, and DSC.
measurements: XRD to detect the presence and proportion of ordered secondary phases versus BCC peaks
TEM and/or atom probe tomography to quantify local chemical ordering and clustering around Al
DSC to identify transformation temperatures and kinetics associated with ordering
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the slow-cooled samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in local chemical ordering or secondary phase formation compared to the rapidly quenched samples, or if the transformation signatures (thermal events or phase changes) do not correlate with the degree of ordering expected from negative mixing enthalpies, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Abstract: SignificanceWhile high-entropy alloys (HEAs) or complex concentrated alloys are touted as potential game changer alloys, many fundamental gaps remain in our understanding of these alloys. (Mg,Mn,Fe,Co,Ni)O: A rocksalt high-entropy oxide containing divalent Mn and Fe

Abstract: High-entropy oxides (HEOs) have aroused growing interest due to fundamental questions relating to their structure formation, phase stability, and the interplay between configurational disorder and physical and chemical properties. Introducing Fe(II) and Mn(II) into a rocksalt HEO is considered challenging, as theoretical analysis suggests that they are unstable in this structure under ambient conditions. Here, we develop a bottom-up method for synthesizing Mn- and Fe-containing rocksalt HEO (FeO-HEO). We present a comprehensive investigation of its crystal structure and the random cation-site occupancy. We show the improved structural robustness of this FeO-HEO and verify the viability of an oxygen sublattice as a buffer layer. Compositional analysis reveals the valence and spin state of the iron species. We further report the antiferromagnetic order of this FeO-HEO below the transition temperature ~218 K and predict the conditions of phase stability of Mn- and Fe-containing HEOs. Entropy-stabilized oxides

Abstract: Configurational disorder can be compositionally engineered into mixed oxide by populating a single sublattice with many distinct cations. The formulations promote novel and entropy-stabilized forms of crystalline matter where metal cations are incorporated in new ways. Here, through rigorous experiments, a simple thermodynamic model, and a five-component oxide formulation, we demonstrate beyond reasonable doubt that entropy predominates the thermodynamic landscape, and drives a reversible solid-state transformation between a multiphase and single-phase state. In the latter, cation distributions are proven to be random and homogeneous. The findings validate the hypothesis that deliberate configurational disorder provides an orthogonal strategy to imagine and discover new phases of crystalline matter and untapped opportunities for property engineering. The composition of oxide compounds controls many of their properties and electronic phases. Here, the authors show that entropy and configurational disorder can stabilize new phases of oxides, potentially enabling a better engineering of their properties.

Polymorphism in a high-entropy alloy

Abstract: Polymorphism, which describes the occurrence of different lattice structures in a crystalline material, is a critical phenomenon in materials science and condensed matter physics. Recently, configuration disorder was compositionally engineered into single lattices, leading to the discovery of high-entropy alloys and high-entropy oxides. For these novel entropy-stabilized forms of crystalline matter with extremely high structural stability, is polymorphism still possible? Here by employing in situ high-pressure synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction, we reveal a polymorphic transition from face-centred-cubic (fcc) structure to hexagonal-close-packing (hcp) structure in the prototype CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy. The transition is irreversible, and our in situ high-temperature synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction experiments at different pressures of the retained hcp high-entropy alloy reveal that the fcc phase is a stable polymorph at high temperatures, while the hcp structure is more thermodynamically favourable at lower temperatures. As pressure is increased, the critical temperature for the hcp-to-fcc transformation also rises.

Effect of Cold Rolling on the Phase Transformation Kinetics of an Al0.5CoCrFeNi High-Entropy Alloy

Abstract: AbstractThe solid state phase transformation kinetics of as-cast and cold rolling deformed Al0.5CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys have been investigated by the thermal expansion method. The phase transformed volume fractions are determined from the thermal expansion curve using the lever rule method, and the deformed sample exhibits a much higher transformation rate. Two kinetic parameters, activation energy (E) and kinetic exponent (n) are determined using Kissinger– Akahira–Sunose (KAS) and Johnson–Mehl–Avrami (JMA) method, respectively. Results show that a pre-deformed sample shows a much lower activation energy and higher kinetic exponent compared with the as-cast sample, which are interpreted based on the deformation induced defects that can promote the nucleation and growth process during phase transformation.Keywords: high-entropy alloy, phase transformation, kinetics, deformation, thermal expansion

The Effect of Hf Addition on the Boronizing and Siliciding Behavior of CoCrFeNi High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: The effect of a boronizing and siliciding process on CoCrFeNiHf0.1–0.42 high entropy alloys was examined in this study. When increasing the amount of added Hf in CoCrFeNiHfx, the structure of the alloys gradually transformed from single-phase FCC to firstly Ni7Hf2 + FCC, and finally to C15 Laves and FCC phases. The boronizing/siliciding process resulted in the formation of a silicon-rich layer and a boride layer (BL). Increasing the amount of Hf in the alloys resulted in a decrease in the combined layer thickness, which was measured for CoCrFeNi, CoCrFeNiHf0.1, CoCrFeNiHf0.2, and CoCrFeNiHf0.42 to be 70 µm, 63 µm, 20 µm, and 15 µm, respectively. In contrast, the thickness of the transition zone/diffusion zone increased with more Hf in the alloys. While silicon atoms were gathered close to the BL, they were not transferred into the CoCrFeNi substrate. In contrast to the observation for CoCrFeNi, Si atoms penetrated through the Ni-rich phase (Ni7Hf2) in the CoCrFeNiHfx alloys. The Observation of Cellular Precipitation in an Ni36Co18Cr20Fe19Al7 High-Entropy Alloy after Quenching and Annealing

Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) comprise a minimum of five major elements. These alloys show some special characteristics, such as excellent mechanical and high temperature properties. The development of the HEAs requires a knowledge of phase transformations during alloy making procedures. The phase transformations of an Ni36Co18Cr20Fe19Al7 HEA were studied in this research. The alloy underwent hot forging, cold rolling, annealing at and quenching from 1323 K, and isothermal holding at 873 K. The alloy is a single face-centered cubic (FCC) phase in the as-quenched condition. After annealing at 873 K, not only fine coherent L12 particles precipitated homogeneously in the FCC matrix, but lamellae of FCC and L12 phases also developed from the grain boundaries. Both lamellar FCC and L12 grains have a cubic-on-cubic orientation relationship (OR). The composition of the lamellar L12 phase is Ni60Co8Cr6Fe6Al20, and that of the lamellar FCC phase is Ni31Co15Cr28Fe21Al4.
